text.text: Plan treatment routes from one page. Plan renewals and one-time calls land on the Service visits board, each technician sees their own list under Mine, and Mark done closes a visit. Products shows what to reorder; Invoices shows who owes you.
Homes and businesses on plans, and what they have paid.
Every treatment visit, which technician has it, what it earns and the margin.
Treatment products, traps and safety gear, with counts and reorder levels.
What has been billed, what is paid and what is overdue.
Visits by status, revenue by treatment type and unpaid invoices.
Quarterly plans make the business predictable. Plan routes a month ahead and keep each technician in one area per day.
On the first of each month, list plan customers due that month.
Group them by area and assign one technician per area.
Create each visit with a day and a window.
Text the customer the evening before.
If the customer is not home, treat the exterior, leave a door hanger and reschedule the interior within the week.
Good records protect the customer and the company. Write them at the property, not later.
Date, time on and off, and technician
Save the notes on the visit row and keep local rules in mind. Records follow the legal retention period for your state.
A callback is a second chance. Treat it as free marketing.
Send the same technician when possible.
Look for the cause: entry points, moisture, food.
Record what changed and tell the customer.
Escalate to the route supervisor and offer an inspection with photos before spending more product.
